entries.summary: Builds a curve of ice-volume equivalent sea level (the sea level you would get if only the change in ice volume mattered) from far-field coral and sediment records, corrected for the way the Earth deforms under ice and water. Puts the low point at about 134 m below today, 29 to 21 thousand years ago, and says the main melt ran from about 16.5 to 8.2 thousand years ago at about 12 m per thousand years on average.
entries.method: Far-field sea-level data (Barbados, Sunda Shelf, Tahiti, Huon Peninsula, Great Barrier Reef, East China Sea, Maldives and others) inverted with glacial-isostatic-adjustment models to separate ice volume from local land movement.

entries.summary: Drilled Acropora palmata coral off Barbados and gave the first continuous record of sea level through the last melt. In 1990 Bard, Hamelin and Fairbanks re-dated the corals by uranium-thorium and put the pulses at about 14 and 11 thousand years ago.

claims.text: U-Th dating confirmed two melt-water surges at about 11 and 14 thousand years BP and moved the start of the last deglaciation 3,000 years earlier.

claims.text: The Black Sea shelf was submerged at 9300 calendar years BP by Mediterranean water, abruptly, taking under 40 years.
claims.evidence: Strontium results indicate that the submergence of the Black Sea shelf at 9300 calendar years BP was caused by the ingress of Mediterranean water and was abrupt, taking < 40 years.

contradicts.about: date of the Black Sea shelf flooding
contradicts.detail: 9,300 cal BP (2017) versus 7,150 radiocarbon yr BP (1997).
Comment titled "Comment on 'Compilation of geophysical ... evidence'" by Guillaume Soulet; reply by Yanchilina, Ryan and McManus the same year. Neither abstract was available.

entries.why_it_matters: Still an open question: the newest paper by the original authors moves the date by about 1,000 years or more and keeps the "abrupt" claim; the lake level of about -120 m is a basin-specific number that should not be a global slider setting.

region.name: Bering Strait and Herald Canyon, Chukchi Sea

entries.summary: A dated core from Herald Canyon shows a shift from a near-shore to a Pacific-influenced open-marine setting at about 11 cal ka BP, interpreted as the breaching of the Bering Strait (about 53 m deep today) at meltwater pulse 1b, later than earlier estimates inside the Younger Dryas.
entries.method: Geophysical mapping and a well-dated sediment core from Herald Canyon.

claims.text: The Bering Strait opened at about 11 cal ka BP, corresponding to meltwater pulse 1b, later than several previous studies.
claims.evidence: Our results suggest an initial opening at about 11 cal ka BP in the earliest Holocene, which is later than in several previous studies.

contradicts.about: meltwater pulse 1B and the date the Bering Strait flooded
contradicts.detail: Jakobsson and others: opening about 11 cal ka BP, tied to MWP-1b. Lambeck: no global 1B. Earlier proxy studies cited by Jakobsson put the opening within the Younger Dryas (12.9 to 11.7 cal ka BP).

entries.why_it_matters: A dated "when did the land bridge go" that our presets can be checked against: the strait is about 53 m deep, so at -60 m (our 11.4 ka preset) about 7 m of land still stands above the water, and at 15 m per thousand years the strait floods about 500 years later, near 10.9 ka: within a few hundred years of Jakobsson's 11 cal ka. Local ice-sheet effects at the strait are not included in that sum.

sources.title: Jakobsson and others, Climate of the Past 13, 2017 (OpenAlex abstract)

entries.notes: Abstract read. bbox is an approximation of the Bering Strait to Herald Canyon area.
entries.title: Post-glacial flooding of the Bering Land Bridge dated to 11 cal ka BP based on new geophysical and sediment records

entries.summary: Uses a geochemical record of Pacific nutrient input to the Arctic to show the Bering Strait was open from at least 46,000 to 35,700 years ago. To match this, a sea-level model needs more than half of the LGM peak ice volume to grow after 46 ka, so the land bridge last formed within about 10,000 years of the LGM.
entries.method: Nitrogen-isotope proxy of Pacific input into the Arctic; sea-level model.

claims.text: The Bering Strait was flooded from 46 ka until about 35.7 ka; sea-level estimates before the LGM vary by more than 60 m.
claims.evidence: we find that the Bering Strait was flooded from the beginning of our records at 46 ka until 35.7 - 2.4 + 3.3 ka

contradicts.detail: Farmer and others: pre-LGM estimates "vary by > 60 m" and the strait was open until 35.7 ka. Lambeck: a rapid fall of about 40 m near 30 ka to the -134 m low. The two disagree about when the land bridge first formed.

entries.why_it_matters: Shows the "ice-age low" is a time series with disputed early parts; our globe starts at 21 ka and has nothing earlier, which matters for first-migration claims.
entries.notes: PMC full text read. The article is dated 27 Dec 2022 online and appears in PNAS vol. 120, 2023.
entries.title: The Bering Strait was flooded 10,000 years before the Last Glacial Maximum

entries.summary: The ridge under Lake Huron was a dry-land corridor between north-east Michigan and southern Ontario 9,000 years ago; the Drop 45 Drive Lane is the most complex hunting structure found under the Great Lakes. A 2016 study (67 samples over 50 km2) found sphagnum, rooted spruce and tamarack and 8 to 9 thousand year old charcoal on the drowned surface during the Lake Stanley lowstand (about 10 to 8 ka).
entries.method: Diver and sonar survey, sediment and core sampling, simulation of hunting.

claims.text: About 9,000 years ago the ridge was a dry land corridor connecting Michigan and Ontario; the Drop 45 Drive Lane is the most complex hunting structure found beneath the Great Lakes.
claims.evidence: Nine thousand years ago, the Alpena-Amberley Ridge (AAR) beneath modern Lake Huron was a dry land corridor that connected northeast Michigan to southern Ontario.

entries.why_it_matters: A lake, not the ocean: the lowstand came from lake outlets and isostatic rebound, not from the global sea-level curve, so the ocean slider cannot place it. This is our "lakes do not follow the ocean" limit as a real case.
entries.notes: Abstracts only. The "who" list mixes the two papers. bbox is approximate for the ridge and not in the abstract.
entries.title: A 9,000-year-old caribou hunting structure beneath Lake Huron (and the Lake Stanley lowstand follow-up)

entries.summary: Underwater excavation of a sinkhole in the Aucilla River, Florida, about 9 m deep and about 11.5 km inland of today's Gulf coast, dates stone tools and mastodon remains to 14,550 calendar years BP, the oldest human occupation in the region.
entries.method: Scuba excavation, 71 new radiocarbon dates and geoarchaeology (as reported in press coverage).

claims.text: Page-Ladson shows occupation of the North American Gulf Coastal Plain at 14,550 B.P.
claims.evidence: Page-Ladson, Florida, provides evidence of the oldest human occupation in the North American Gulf Coastal Plain at 14,550 B.P.

entries.why_it_matters: A Florida site that was dry land at 14,550 years ago when global sea level was about -95 m and the Gulf coast was far out on the shelf; it shows rivers and sinkholes, not the shelf edge, are where the finds are. Depth and distance from the coast are from press reports, not the paper.
entries.notes: Crossref gave a one-sentence abstract. The 9 m depth and 11.5 km inland come from a search summary of press coverage, not a page I opened. bbox is an approximate box for the Aucilla River near the Gulf coast.
entries.title: Pre-Clovis occupation 14,550 years ago at the Page-Ladson site, Florida, and the peopling of the Americas

entries.summary: Compares last-interglacial sea-level indicators across the Bahamian islands with Earth-deformation models, because the elevation of those features also records local uplift or subsidence due to the growth and decay of ice sheets. Used here as evidence of how strongly local ice-sheet effects change the apparent height of old sea levels in the Bahamas.
entries.method: Field elevations of fossil marine sediments and reefs compared with Earth deformation models.

claims.text: The elevations of past sea-level features also record local uplift or subsidence due to the growth and decay of ice sheets.
claims.evidence: However, the elevations of these features also record local uplift or subsidence due to the growth and decay of ice sheets since the time of deposition.

entries.why_it_matters: About the last interglacial (130 to 116 thousand years ago), not the last ice age, so it gives the mechanism for the Bahamas but not an ice-age figure; I did not find a published LGM relative-sea-level number for the Bahamas or Florida.

entries.title: Sea-level trends across The Bahamas constrain peak last interglacial ice melt

entries.summary: Reports a thin layer at about 50 Clovis-age sites in North America, dated about 12.9 ka, with magnetic grains with iridium, microspherules, charcoal, soot, carbon spherules with nanodiamonds and fullerenes with extraterrestrial helium, and argues an impact caused Younger Dryas cooling, extinctions and the end of Clovis. It is the paper that started the Younger Dryas impact hypothesis (YDIH).
entries.method: Geochemical and microscopic analysis of sediments from Clovis-age sites and Carolina Bays.

claims.text: A thin layer at about 12.9 ka at Clovis-age sites carries seven markers the authors say are evidence of an extraterrestrial impact and biomass burning.
claims.evidence: all of which are evidence for an ET impact and associated biomass burning at approximately 12.9 ka

contradicts.about: iridium at the Younger Dryas boundary
contradicts.detail: Firestone and others: layers with iridium-bearing magnetic grains. Paquay and others: "our results do not reproduce the previously reported elevated Ir concentrations".

entries.why_it_matters: Legend-makers tie Atlantis (Plato's date, about 9600 BCE) to this impact; the impact claim is contested, and it has no connection to where the sea stood.

sources.title: Firestone and others, PNAS 104, 2007 (OpenAlex abstract, PMC copy at PMC1994902)

entries.notes: Abstract read. The link to Atlantis is through the Younger Dryas date; Plato does not mention an impact.
entries.title: Evidence for an extraterrestrial impact 12,900 years ago that contributed to the megafaunal extinctions and the Younger Dryas cooling

entries.summary: Measured platinum-group elements, gold and osmium isotopes in matching terrestrial, lake and marine sections and found no iridium anomaly, crustal osmium ratios, and no marine anomaly in the Gulf of California or the Cariaco Basin.
entries.method: Geochemistry on sections from North America and one in Belgium.

claims.text: Results do not reproduce the elevated iridium reported by Firestone and others and show no extraterrestrial platinum-group anomaly.
claims.evidence: First, our results do not reproduce the previously reported elevated Ir concentrations.

contradicts.detail: See entry.

entries.why_it_matters: The first published reply; a good example of a reply by a different lab on the same layers.
entries.notes: Abstract read.
entries.title: Absence of geochemical evidence for an impact event at the Bølling–Allerød/Younger Dryas transition

entries.summary: A very long review arguing the YDIH has no self-consistent scenario, no crater dated to the onset of the Younger Dryas, and that the nano- to microscale evidence (charcoal, spherules, nanodiamonds, platinum) has identification, measurement and interpretation problems and is associated with ordinary terrestrial processes. Sweatman, Powell and West (Airbursts and Cratering Impacts, 2024) call it a "Gish gallop" and say the hypothesis stands on more than 50 sites on five continents; Holliday and others replied in Earth-Science Reviews in 2024.
entries.method: Review of the impact, geochemical, archaeological and palaeoecological literature.

claims.text: No craters have been identified that date to the onset of the Younger Dryas, and most purported indicators are associated with terrestrial processes.
claims.evidence: No craters have been identified that date to the onset of the Younger Dryas.

claims.text: The YDIH has been corroborated by scores of articles at more than 50 Younger Dryas boundary sites on five continents (the proponents' reply).
claims.evidence: it has been corroborated by scores of articles in dozens of peer-reviewed journals based on the discovery of some combination of synchronous nanodiamonds, exotic microspherules and platinum enrichment at more than 50 Younger Dryas boundary sites on five continents

contradicts.about: whether the Younger Dryas impact hypothesis is refuted
contradicts.detail: Holliday and others (2023): refuted, with no craters and unreliable markers. Sweatman, Powell and West (2024): "well established", with shocked quartz and more than 50 sites. Holliday and others answered in Earth-Science Reviews in 2024 (abstract not available to me).

entries.why_it_matters: The standing state of the debate in 2024: still contested by the people on each side; any copy on a/lost that mentions it should say "disputed" and not endorse either.

sources.title: Holliday and others, Earth-Science Reviews, 2023 (OpenAlex abstract)

entries.notes: Abstract read. The abstract in my read was truncated.
entries.title: Comprehensive refutation of the Younger Dryas Impact Hypothesis (YDIH)

entries.summary: A line-by-line reply saying Holliday and others' 96,000-word article gives no new evidence, shows poor understanding of uncertainty in data, and that the hypothesis remains strong, with shocked quartz now added. Published in Airbursts and Cratering Impacts.
entries.method: Critical analysis of selected portions of the Holliday article.

contradicts.detail: See entry.

who: A. J. T. Jull and others
entries.summary: Tree-ring radiocarbon over 1700 to 1500 BCE shows an offset from the standard calibration curve, shifting the radiocarbon date for the Thera eruption toward the 16th century BCE and narrowing the gap with archaeological dating (mid 16th to early 15th century BCE). Manning (2022) combines 14C, stratigraphy and Bayesian models to give 1606 to 1589 BCE (68.3%) or 1609 to 1560 BCE (95.4%), in the Second Intermediate Period in Egypt.
entries.method: Annual-resolution radiocarbon series from calendar-dated tree rings; Bayesian chronology (Manning).

claims.text: Eruption date range shifts toward the 16th century BCE; radiocarbon had said late 17th to early 16th, archaeology mid 16th to early 15th.
claims.evidence: a discrepancy between radiocarbon (late 17th-early 16th century BCE) and archaeological (mid 16th-early 15th century BCE) dating evidence for Thera
This enables a robust high-resolution dating for the eruption ~1606-1589 BCE (68.3% probability), ~1609-1560 BCE (95.4% probability).

contradicts.with: Archaeological date (mid 16th to early 15th century BCE)
contradicts.detail: Radiocarbon and Bayesian work (Manning 2022): 1609 to 1560 BCE at 95%. Older archaeological date: mid 16th to early 15th century BCE, about 1500 BCE. Pearson and others: shifts the radiocarbon range toward the 16th century BCE.

entries.why_it_matters: Thera is a place for Atlantis and the Minoans, around 3,500 years ago when the sea was already at today's level (within a few metres), so the sea-level slider is not relevant to it; a legend card should state the date range.

sources.title: Pearson and others, Science Advances, 2018 (OpenAlex abstract)

entries.notes: Abstracts read. Author names are from OpenAlex. The statement that the sea was within a few metres of today at 3,500 years ago is my reading of Lambeck's "ocean volumes remained nearly constant" after about 2.5 ka; not independently checked.
entries.title: Annual radiocarbon record indicates 16th century BCE date for the Thera eruption (with Manning 2022)

entries.summary: Collina-Girard (2001, in French) proposed that Plato's Atlantis matches a palaeo-island on Spartel Bank in the Strait of Gibraltar, drowned as the ice-age sea rose. Gutscher (2005) compares Plato's description with new multibeam bathymetry of the island, argues a great earthquake and tsunami (M above 8.5) around 11.6 ka matches the story, and points to an unusually thick turbidite dated about 12 ka in the Gulf of Cadiz. He says the island could have been inhabited then; he later said it could not have been Atlantis because Plato's society was Bronze Age.
entries.method: High-resolution bathymetric map of the bank; comparison with Plato; Gulf of Cadiz turbidite record.

claims.text: A catastrophic submergence of the Spartel palaeo-island at about 11.6 ka matches a great earthquake and tsunami; a thick turbidite dated about 12 ka may coincide.
claims.evidence: An unusually thick turbidite dated as ca. 12 ka may coincide with the destructive event in Plato's account.

contradicts.with: Review in Bryn Mawr Classical Review (as quoted by Wikipedia)
contradicts.about: whether Spartel Bank is Plato's Atlantis
contradicts.detail: Collina-Girard and Gutscher: a candidate. A Bryn Mawr Classical Review review (as quoted on Wikipedia): Collina-Girard "has certainly succeeded in throwing some light upon some momentous developments in human prehistory ... Just as certainly, however, he has not found Plato's Atlantis." I did not read the review.

entries.why_it_matters: The one Atlantis candidate that is driven by sea level: the bank's summit is now about 56 m under water, so at -60 m (our 11.4 ka preset) it is a rocky islet a few metres high and at -95 m a larger island; our grid cannot resolve a bank of that size.

sources.title: Collina-Girard, C. R. Acad. Sci. IIA 333, 2001 (record only)

entries.notes: Gutscher abstract read; Collina-Girard's abstract not available. The 56 m summit depth is from Wikipedia, which cites the bathymetry; the "could not have been Atlantis" remark is from the same page and I did not find Gutscher's own text.
entries.title: Destruction of Atlantis by a great earthquake and tsunami? A geological analysis of the Spartel Bank hypothesis (and Collina-Girard 2001)

who: Richard Freund and team (2011 television special)
entries.summary: In 2004 Rainer Kühne published a satellite-image observation of ring-like features in the Guadalquivir marshes as a possible "Atlantis" (Antiquity project gallery). In 2011 a US television special reported a Freund-led expedition with ground-penetrating radar, resistivity and magnetometry in Doñana National Park, saying it found a communal oven and canal traces and a tsunami-buried 4,000-year-old civilization. Spanish scientists quoted in the press said they do not "go in for farfetched interpretations".
entries.method: Satellite imagery; ground-penetrating radar, electrical resistivity tomography and magnetometry (reported in a press article).

claims.text: Researchers said they found proof of a 4,000-year-old civilization buried by a tsunami in the Doñana marshes.
claims.evidence: Scientists say they have found proof of a 4,000-year-old civilization that was buried by a tsunami.

contradicts.with: Juan Villarias-Robles (Spanish anthropologist, via a search summary)
contradicts.detail: Freund presented the work; Villarias-Robles, who worked on the site, said (in a source I did not fetch) that Freund did not lead the investigations and spent less than a week there.

entries.why_it_matters: The claim is press and television, with one short Antiquity gallery note behind it; I found no peer-reviewed paper reporting the 2011 results. Treat as unverified.

sources.title: Popular Science, "Scientists Say They May Have Found Lost City of Atlantis Near Spain", 2011

entries.notes: The press page was read; Kühne's note was not opened (Cambridge link failed). The Villarias-Robles criticism comes from a search summary of Spanish-language press, not a fetched page.
entries.title: A location for "Atlantis"? (Kühne 2004) and the 2011 Doñana expedition claim

entries.summary: Describes the Richat Structure as a dome at least 40 km across with three nested rings and a kilometre-scale breccia, and proposes that it is the surface expression of a Cretaceous alkaline complex with hydrothermal karst at its summit. A 2024 Lithos paper by Abdeina and others on its "polyphase history" and igneous origin has the same view of origin.
entries.method: Field geology and mineralogy.

claims.text: The Richat structure is the surface expression of a Cretaceous alkaline complex, not an impact crater.
claims.evidence: The circular Richat structure and its breccia core thus represent the superficial expression of a Cretaceous alkaline complex with an exceptionally well preserved hydrothermal karst infilling at its summit.

entries.why_it_matters: The Richat structure is about 40 km across and roughly 550 km inland of the Atlantic coast at 21 N; sea level has nothing to do with it, which is the strongest argument against its use in a drowned-land context.
entries.notes: Abstract read; the 2024 paper's abstract was not available to me, so "same view of origin" rests on its title ("igneous Richat Structure"). The 550 km figure is my estimate from the structure's coordinates (21.12 N, 11.40 W) and the coast near 17 W, not sourced.
entries.title: Resolving the Richat enigma: Doming and hydrothermal karstification above an alkaline complex

gaps: A published, open, side-by-side check of how far one global sea level misplaces coasts against local (glacial-isostatic) sea level, for the places the public asks about. I found papers that state the local figure for one place (Yokoyama for the Great Barrier Reef, Sathiamurthy and Voris for the Sunda Shelf) but no comparison across places. The sensitivity table in this lane is my own count.

A downloadable, fine-grid, local-sea-level paleo-topography that covers the last 21,000 years at steps short enough for the fast melt. A survey of the floor of the Persian Gulf. Rose (2010) proposes a "Gulf Oasis" from reasoning about sea level and archaeology on the coasts; I found no paper reporting a site on the Gulf floor.
A peer-reviewed report of the 2011 Doñana "Atlantis" expedition. I found a 2004 Antiquity project-gallery note, a 2011 television special and press coverage only.

A global list of known submerged prehistoric sites. SPLASHCOS covers Europe (and I could not open its viewer); Australia's first confirmed shelf sites were reported only in 2020. I found no list that covers the world.
A shoreline dataset for the last 21,000 years that carries uncertainty. EMODnet Geology rates confidence per line in Europe; I found nothing similar outside Europe.
A resolution of the meltwater pulse 1B dispute (Barbados for, Tahiti and the global composite against) and of the size of meltwater pulse 1A (8 to 22 m depending on the study).
